sources.title: Trump launches Super Intelligence Force to keep U.S. leading AI, names top officials
passages: President Donald Trump announced a new Super Intelligence Force (SIF) on Sunday and has already picked members who will lead the charge on AI in America.

"We’re going to be signing a document today at about 5 o’clock, renaming artificial intelligence, because it’s not artificial, we all agree on that," Trump said, "we're going to be renaming it super intelligence." Trump's full embrace of the use of artificial intelligence comes as Democrats have called for a halt to further developing the technology over fears it will put Americans out of work or at a disadvantage.
Trump made the announcement on Truth Social this morning, describing that the task force was created in response to his White House Accord on Super Intelligence that he hosted the previous week.

The site is designed to help citizens access federal information and services, such as filling out passport applications online and enrolling in Medicaid. 'Anyone who has used Grok or Gemini or ChatGPT will understand instantly how to use America.gov,' Trump said at an event unveiling the new website.

White House officials have stressed the importance of AI pushing ahead despite those concerns, explaining that American technologists must lead the AI boom to prevent China or other rivals from dominating the space.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump announced a new Super Intelligence Force (SIF) on Sunday and has already picked members who will lead the charge on AI in America. According to Trump, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will lead the task force alongside Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission, Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael and the Director of the Office of Personnel Management, Scott Kupor. The task force is in charge of coordinating the government's engagement with religious organizations, superintelligence providers, consumers and AI companies. Trump said SIF will ensure that America continues to lead the world on AI, which he says, "is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans.' The team, which is led by Clayton, will report to Trump and the White House Chief of Staff, Susie Wiles. Trump made the announcement on Truth Social this morning, describing that the task force was created in response to his White House Accord on Super Intelligence that he hosted the previous week. The president summoned the world's most powerful tech executives to the White House on Tuesday, where he announced that he would be renaming artificial intelligence to super intelligence in all further government communications. "We’re going to be signing a document today at about 5 o’clock, renaming artificial intelligence, because it’s not artificial, we all agree on that," Trump said, "we're going to be renaming it super intelligence." Trump's full embrace of the use of artificial intelligence comes as Democrats have called for a halt to further developing the technology over fears it will put Americans out of work or at a disadvantage. White House officials have stressed the importance of AI pushing ahead despite those concerns, explaining that American technologists must lead the AI boom to prevent China or other rivals from dominating the space. Earlier the same day, the administration rolled out an AI-powered website, America.gov. The site is designed to help citizens access federal information and services, such as filling out passport applications online and enrolling in Medicaid. 'Anyone who has used Grok or Gemini or ChatGPT will understand instantly how to use America.gov,' Trump said at an event unveiling the new website.

sources.title: Trump vows to create ‘AI Force’ and appoint czar amid calls to regulate technology’s development
passages: President Donald Trump said Saturday he plans to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the rapid development of artificial intelligence.

AI’s meteoric growth has led to major stock market gains and buoyed the manufacturing sector through the construction of data centers — which Trump calls “the golden goose.” Yet fears about the technology’s potential to eliminate jobs and AI data centers’ impact on communities have led to a souring in public sentiment.
Trump’s creation of the Space Force in 2019 marked the first new US military service since 1947.
“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” Trump said in his post Saturday.

Government has to be regulating this.” Venture capitalist David Sacks served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March, when he stepped down after reaching his time limit as a special government employee.
A White House official also said that AI safety would be “on the agenda” when Trump meets with Xi.

“We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!” Trump has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns.
CNN previously reported that Trump officials were contemplating a meeting with major technology and AI chiefs on the sidelines of the high-stakes summit, though nothing has been finalized.
Trump’s announcement comes as the White House and Congress have faced pressure in recent weeks to enact AI safeguards.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump said Saturday he plans to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the rapid development of artificial intelligence. The president, writing on Truth Social, repeated his assessment that fears over AI amount to a hoax and also seemed to acknowledge some of the risks the technology presents, saying, “we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System.” “For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ — Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” Trump said in the post. CNN has reached out to the White House for more details on the AI czar’s duties, whether the president has anyone in mind for the role, and whether the “AI Force” will be a branch of the military, like the Space Force. Trump’s creation of the Space Force in 2019 marked the first new US military service since 1947. Trump’s announcement comes as the White House and Congress have faced pressure in recent weeks to enact AI safeguards. The president has downplayed concerns, claiming that a “SICK conspiracy” was afoot to undermine AI. “We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” Trump said in his post Saturday. “We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!” Trump has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns. The issue has quickly come to dominate political debate in the United States, after industry leaders called for a global slowdown in development. AI’s meteoric growth has led to major stock market gains and buoyed the manufacturing sector through the construction of data centers — which Trump calls “the golden goose.” Yet fears about the technology’s potential to eliminate jobs and AI data centers’ impact on communities have led to a souring in public sentiment. Democrats have been more vocal in their calls to slow AI development, with former President Barack Obama urging potential Democratic presidential candidates to put AI at the center of their agendas in 2028. “My view this week has been it is good that some of the leading companies have said we need to slow this down, and we should encourage that,” Obama said Friday during a fireside chat at Colgate University, according to excerpts of his speech obtained by CNN. “There have been some on the left who’ve said we shouldn’t allow them to make that decision. Government has to be regulating this.” Venture capitalist David Sacks served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March, when he stepped down after reaching his time limit as a special government employee. He now chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. The Trump administration will convene a high-level event on AI on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, multiple sources familiar with the matter previously told CNN. A day later, several technology executives — including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Google’s Sundar Pichai — will attend a state dinner at the White House as part of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, according to a White House official. CNN previously reported that Trump officials were contemplating a meeting with major technology and AI chiefs on the sidelines of the high-stakes summit, though nothing has been finalized. The president, writing on Truth Social, repeated his assessment that fears over AI amount to a hoax and also seemed to acknowledge some of the risks the technology presents, saying, “we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System.” “For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term.
To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ — Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” Trump said in the post.

CNN has reached out to the White House for more details on the AI czar’s duties, whether the president has anyone in mind for the role, and whether the “AI Force” will be a branch of the military, like the Space Force.
Trump’s creation of the Space Force in 2019 marked the first new US military service since 1947.
Trump’s announcement comes as the White House and Congress have faced pressure in recent weeks to enact AI safeguards.
The president has downplayed concerns, claiming that a “SICK conspiracy” was afoot to undermine AI.
“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” Trump said in his post Saturday.

“We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!” Trump has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns.
The issue has quickly come to dominate political debate in the United States, after industry leaders called for a global slowdown in development.

AI’s meteoric growth has led to major stock market gains and buoyed the manufacturing sector through the construction of data centers — which Trump calls “the golden goose.” Yet fears about the technology’s potential to eliminate jobs and AI data centers’ impact on communities have led to a souring in public sentiment.

Democrats have been more vocal in their calls to slow AI development, with former President Barack Obama urging potential Democratic presidential candidates to put AI at the center of their agendas in 2028.

“My view this week has been it is good that some of the leading companies have said we need to slow this down, and we should encourage that,” Obama said Friday during a fireside chat at Colgate University, according to excerpts of his speech obtained by CNN.
“There have been some on the left who’ve said we shouldn’t allow them to make that decision.

Government has to be regulating this.” Venture capitalist David Sacks served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March, when he stepped down after reaching his time limit as a special government employee.
He now chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
The Trump administration will convene a high-level event on AI on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, multiple sources familiar with the matter previously told CNN.

A day later, several technology executives — including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Google’s Sundar Pichai — will attend a state dinner at the White House as part of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, according to a White House official.
CNN previously reported that Trump officials were contemplating a meeting with major technology and AI chiefs on the sidelines of the high-stakes summit, though nothing has been finalized.
A White House official also said that AI safety would be “on the agenda” when Trump meets with Xi.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump announced a new "Super Intelligence Force" in a post on Truth Social Sunday, just days after signing an executive order renaming Artificial Intelligence. Trump says the force will "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence," by coordinating the federal government's efforts. "The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump said on Truth Social. He said the force will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering and Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael, and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor will all serve as vice chairs. Clayton spoke with The Wall Street Journal about the force, saying, "The president asked that a group be put together." He said the panel has been tasked with reporting on the risks and opportunities AI poses within 120 days, and emphasized the U.S. government's desire to lead the industry, saying "the risk of not being first is high." According to The Journal, the force will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms, checking them for breaches, hacks and other incidents and issues. The Journal says in addition to Clayton and the vice chairs, Super Intelligence Force members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. Super Intelligence vs AI The force is just the latest effort Trump has made, using the term superintelligence rather than artificial intelligence. During a UN General Assembly meeting last month, Trump said the word artificial "makes it sound fake, and it is not fake, it's actually amazing." Since then, he's signed an executive order directing the U.S. government to officially rebrand AI as "super intelligence" in federal communications.

CNN reported Friday that Trump was expected to tap Clayton to lead the group. The president has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns, and previously referred to fears over AI as being a “hoax.” His support for the technology comes amid widespread frustrations over the data centers used to support it, which are shaking up midterm races. The president hosted top AI executives at the White House last week. extraction.body: President Donald Trump formally announced the creation of what he called a “Super Intelligence Force,” an artificial intelligence task force that he says will work to promote AI dominance while also protecting American lives and interests. "The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans,” Trump wrote on his social media platform Sunday. Trump's announcement was thin on details, with the president not outlining any specific action or oversight the task force will have on AI development -- an issue about which some tech CEOs have raised concerns and called for federal regulation. "The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump added. An ABC News request sent to the White House for more information about the task force's objectives did not immediately receive a response. Trump says AI leaders signed a 'constitution' to police themselves Last month, Trump said he would create an AI task force amid rising concerns about the technology. Sunday's formal announcement comes after the president met with top tech CEOs at the White House last week, where he said he and six companies signed a "constitution" establishing standards on how to self-police their technology. Trump said the task force will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, as well as Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor. Clayton, who is expected to serve as the White House's new AI czar, told The Wall Street Journal in an interview published Saturday that global dominance in AI makes the U.S. more equipped to address risks from adversaries, echoing the president’s support for the technology's continued growth. "The risk of not being first is high," Clayton told The Wall Street Journal. “Not being first increases the identified, and unidentified, risks, particularly from our adversaries. Being first will better enable us to address those risks on behalf of the American people." Clayton said of the AI task force, "I expect there will be mechanisms developed in dialogue, just like there are in other industries." According to The Wall Street Journal, Clayton cited risk models for the financial industry that have been developed in conjunction with the Federal Reserve and Securities and Exchange Commission. He told the newspaper that the task force would examine current law and discuss possible actions that Congress could take. Bill Gates diagnoses problems with AI, but an expert questions his prescription Clayton also expressed confidence in the group that the president has appointed to run the AI task force, citing the "diverse skill sets" and "common commitment" of its members. "These are all serious people who have addressed opportunities and risks in the past and are committed to doing this so that America wins the AI race and we win it through the benefit of the American people," he added.

Trump said the task force will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, as well as Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor.

"The risk of not being first is high," Clayton told The Wall Street Journal. “Not being first increases the identified, and unidentified, risks, particularly from our adversaries. Being first will better enable us to address those risks on behalf of the American people."
Clayton said of the AI task force, "I expect there will be mechanisms developed in dialogue, just like there are in other industries."

According to The Wall Street Journal, Clayton cited risk models for the financial industry that have been developed in conjunction with the Federal Reserve and Securities and Exchange Commission. He told the newspaper that the task force would examine current law and discuss possible actions that Congress could take.

Clayton also expressed confidence in the group that the president has appointed to run the AI task force, citing the "diverse skill sets" and "common commitment" of its members.

"These are all serious people who have addressed opportunities and risks in the past and are committed to doing this so that America wins the AI race and we win it through the benefit of the American people," he added.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump announced a new "Super Intelligence Force" in a post on Truth Social Sunday, just days after signing an executive order renaming Artificial Intelligence. Trump says the force will "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence," by coordinating the federal government's efforts. "The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump said on Truth Social. He said the force will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering and Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael, and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor will all serve as vice chairs. Clayton spoke with The Wall Street Journal about the force, saying, "The president asked that a group be put together." He said the panel has been tasked with reporting on the risks and opportunities AI poses within 120 days, and emphasized the U.S. government's desire to lead the industry, saying "the risk of not being first is high." According to The Journal, the force will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms, checking them for breaches, hacks and other incidents and issues. The Journal says in addition to Clayton and the vice chairs, Super Intelligence Force members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. Super Intelligence vs AI The force is just the latest effort Trump has made, using the term superintelligence rather than artificial intelligence. During a UN General Assembly meeting last month, Trump said the word artificial "makes it sound fake, and it is not fake, it's actually amazing." Since then, he's signed an executive order directing the U.S. government to officially rebrand AI as "super intelligence" in federal communications.

Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review."
Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics).

extraction.body: President Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as his new "AI czar," adding a different category of intelligence, the "artificial" kind, to the U.S. spy chief's portfolio. In a post on Truth Social , Trump said Clayton will lead a newly formed "Super Intelligence Force" alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor. The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans." Clayton will keep his job as DNI, which oversees the nation's 18 intelligence agencies. Trump's announcement follows meeting last Tuesday at the White House where top AI executives signed what he called a " morally binding " agreement to police themselves in order to prevent their increasingly powerful models from going rogue and harming humanity . "There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said at the meeting. "This is going to be all for the good, and we're going to have it be nice and safe." Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are " Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers ." "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he wrote on social media . Elsewhere, Trump has said that regulation would handicap the U.S. in its race to "win" AI. "Whoever wins AI ... that's the group that wins," Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month . "We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way." According to the Guardian , Trump's previous AI and crypto czar, billionaire tech investor David Sacks, consistently "counseled the president to give a soft touch to AI regulation, helping push executive orders and other measures aimed at loosening restrictions on the technology." Sacks also "maintains direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies," the paper reported, though he took steps to divest some of his holdings last year while serving in the administration. He stepped down in March. Will Clayton follow Sacks's lead? Or will he chart a new course? Here's what we know so far. Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics). As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings. During Trump's first term, from 2017 to 2020, Clayton chaired the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management . (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.) In late 2024, Trump nominated Clayton to serve as U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, his first prosecutorial job; Trump later appointed Clayton to serve in an acting capacity after New York Sen. Chuck Schumer blocked his appointment. Reports suggest Clayton was also considered for roles as secretary of the treasury, attorney general and director of the Central Intelligence Agency. In November 2025, Trump ordered the Department of Justice to investigate Democrats associated with Jeffrey Epstein, and U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi assigned Clayton to lead the probe . After former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard resigned in May 2026, Trump tapped Clayton to replace her. "He's very qualified," Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia said at the time . But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support. "I'm not an election denier," Clayton told the Senate. "He went through our processes, and Joe Biden became the president of the United States." During his DNI confirmation hearings, Clayton described AI as "a game changer ," warning that it represents "not only an opportunity but a threat." "We should just all recognize that," he continued. "When something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it." On Tuesday, Clayton attended Trump's White House meeting with top AI executives. Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence " — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S. AI development. "Super intelligence is a national security issue, and that was something that was recognized yesterday by not just the industry leaders but everybody in the room," Clayton said. "But to, in some way, not try to drive forward inside the United States, with companies that are regulated in the United States ... to somehow say we should back away from this and let the rest of the world develop these models and implement these models? I don't think anybody in that room, and I don't think any American, should think that that's a good strategy." Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts that Trump's current policy of letting AI companies police themselves will prove to be "a recipe for disaster," Clayton suggested that the U.S. government's existing regulatory framework could also help keep AI in check. "My response to the American people on that front is we have a Federal Trade Commission, we have a Department of Justice," Clayton said. "I know the leaders of both those organizations, and they're committed to protecting the American people in this regard." According to Trump's post, the Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the federal government's dealings with AI companies, infrastructure providers, consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, CNN reported . Last month, Trump wrote on social media that he would "be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar.' "Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he added. In the same post, the president again dismissed concerns about AI safety as a "hoax" perpetrated by "Radical Left Democrats." He also wrote that going forward, his administration would not "in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," which he described as "the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet" — only "even larger and more impactful." "Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump explained. As for reining in "bad" actors, he wrote, "we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System." Clayton, it seems, will now be in charge of cherishing, helping and watching over the AI industry as it grows. He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job . "He's right here. That's a good idea." It's unclear what happened to a separate idea Trump floated last month, which he called "the AI Force." "I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force , which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote in his September social media post about naming an AI czar. According to Axios , Trump's AI Force idea "caught advisers by surprise," setting off "a mad dash" within the administration "to imagine what AI Force would look like." When Sacks served as AI czar, he repeatedly persuaded the president and his administration to resist new AI restrictions, including state laws to limit AI . Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review." The Wall Street Journal recently reported the Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles were "caught off guard and unhappy" with Trump's decision after they "spent months negotiating to increase oversight of AI and had consulted a range of industry executives on the order." According to the Journal's sources, Wiles "told others that Sacks had persuaded Trump" to back down "in a last-minute call," leaving Bessent "worried that AI-led cyberattacks could wreak havoc on the nation's banking system."

Musk said on his social media platform X that SI was “better” than AI – and that he was renaming his aerospace company’s AI unit from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI.

coreStoryFacts.text: President Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as his new "AI czar," adding a different category of intelligence, the "artificial" kind, to the U.S. spy chief's portfolio.

Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review."
Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics).
As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings.

From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management . (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.)

In a post on Truth Social , Trump said Clayton will lead a newly formed "Super Intelligence Force" alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor.
The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans."

Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are " Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers ."
But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support.
In late 2024, Trump nominated Clayton to serve as U.S.

Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence " — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S.
"I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force , which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote in his September social media post about naming an AI czar.
Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen.
Clayton, it seems, will now be in charge of cherishing, helping and watching over the AI industry as it grows.
He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job .
According to Axios , Trump's AI Force idea "caught advisers by surprise," setting off "a mad dash" within the administration "to imagine what AI Force would look like."
"Whoever wins AI ... that's the group that wins," Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month .
"We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way."
As for reining in "bad" actors, he wrote, "we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System."

In the same post, the president again dismissed concerns about AI safety as a "hoax" perpetrated by "Radical Left Democrats." He also wrote that going forward, his administration would not "in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," which he described as "the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet" — only "even larger and more impactful."

extraction.body: President Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as his new "AI czar," adding a different category of intelligence, the "artificial" kind, to the U.S. spy chief's portfolio. In a post on Truth Social , Trump said Clayton will lead a newly formed "Super Intelligence Force" alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor. The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans." Clayton will keep his job as DNI, which oversees the nation's 18 intelligence agencies. Trump's announcement follows meeting last Tuesday at the White House where top AI executives signed what he called a " morally binding " agreement to police themselves in order to prevent their increasingly powerful models from going rogue and harming humanity . "There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said at the meeting. "This is going to be all for the good, and we're going to have it be nice and safe." Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are " Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers ." "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he wrote on social media . Elsewhere, Trump has said that regulation would handicap the U.S. in its race to "win" AI. "Whoever wins AI ... that's the group that wins," Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month . "We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way." According to the Guardian , Trump's previous AI and crypto czar, billionaire tech investor David Sacks, consistently "counseled the president to give a soft touch to AI regulation, helping push executive orders and other measures aimed at loosening restrictions on the technology." Sacks also "maintains direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies," the paper reported, though he took steps to divest some of his holdings last year while serving in the administration. He stepped down in March. Will Clayton follow Sacks's lead? Or will he chart a new course? Here's what we know so far. Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics). As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings. During Trump's first term, from 2017 to 2020, Clayton chaired the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management . (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.) In late 2024, Trump nominated Clayton to serve as U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, his first prosecutorial job; Trump later appointed Clayton to serve in an acting capacity after New York Sen. Chuck Schumer blocked his appointment. Reports suggest Clayton was also considered for roles as secretary of the treasury, attorney general and director of the Central Intelligence Agency. In November 2025, Trump ordered the Department of Justice to investigate Democrats associated with Jeffrey Epstein, and U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi assigned Clayton to lead the probe . After former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard resigned in May 2026, Trump tapped Clayton to replace her. "He's very qualified," Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia said at the time . But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support. "I'm not an election denier," Clayton told the Senate. "He went through our processes, and Joe Biden became the president of the United States." During his DNI confirmation hearings, Clayton described AI as "a game changer ," warning that it represents "not only an opportunity but a threat." "We should just all recognize that," he continued. "When something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it." On Tuesday, Clayton attended Trump's White House meeting with top AI executives. Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence " — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S. AI development. "Super intelligence is a national security issue, and that was something that was recognized yesterday by not just the industry leaders but everybody in the room," Clayton said. "But to, in some way, not try to drive forward inside the United States, with companies that are regulated in the United States ... to somehow say we should back away from this and let the rest of the world develop these models and implement these models? I don't think anybody in that room, and I don't think any American, should think that that's a good strategy." Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts that Trump's current policy of letting AI companies police themselves will prove to be "a recipe for disaster," Clayton suggested that the U.S. government's existing regulatory framework could also help keep AI in check. "My response to the American people on that front is we have a Federal Trade Commission, we have a Department of Justice," Clayton said. "I know the leaders of both those organizations, and they're committed to protecting the American people in this regard." According to Trump's post, the Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the federal government's dealings with AI companies, infrastructure providers, consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, CNN reported . Last month, Trump wrote on social media that he would "be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar.' "Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he added. In the same post, the president again dismissed concerns about AI safety as a "hoax" perpetrated by "Radical Left Democrats." He also wrote that going forward, his administration would not "in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," which he described as "the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet" — only "even larger and more impactful." "Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump explained. As for reining in "bad" actors, he wrote, "we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System." Clayton, it seems, will now be in charge of cherishing, helping and watching over the AI industry as it grows. He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job . "He's right here. That's a good idea." It's unclear what happened to a separate idea Trump floated last month, which he called "the AI Force." "I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force , which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote in his September social media post about naming an AI czar. According to Axios , Trump's AI Force idea "caught advisers by surprise," setting off "a mad dash" within the administration "to imagine what AI Force would look like." When Sacks served as AI czar, he repeatedly persuaded the president and his administration to resist new AI restrictions, including state laws to limit AI . Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review." The Wall Street Journal recently reported the Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles were "caught off guard and unhappy" with Trump's decision after they "spent months negotiating to increase oversight of AI and had consulted a range of industry executives on the order." According to the Journal's sources, Wiles "told others that Sacks had persuaded Trump" to back down "in a last-minute call," leaving Bessent "worried that AI-led cyberattacks could wreak havoc on the nation's banking system."

passages: US President Donald Trump has appointed Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the administration's AI czar, the Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday, citing an interview with Clayton.
Clayton, who was appointed intelligence chief in August, will lead a new White House panel tasked with reporting within 120 days on the risks and opportunities posed by AI, the newspaper said.

Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter.
Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar role at the beginning of Trump's second term.
Trump has appeared to take a light touch toward AI regulation, arguing that excessive oversight could weaken competitiveness against China.
He said on Tuesday that he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology.

Clayton, who was appointed intelligence chief in August, will lead a new White House panel tasked with reporting within 120 days on the risks and opportunities posed by AI, the newspaper said. "The president asked that a group be put together," which the administration refers to as the "Super Intelligence Force," to ensure the US remains a leader in advanced AI while protecting Americans' interests, Clayton told the Journal, adding that "the risk of not being first is high." The safety of AI has become a major issue in recent weeks, with some researchers warning that people building the technology believe it could kill humans within a decade. Several Democratic and Republican lawmakers have responded with alarm and calls for more action. Trump has appeared to take a light touch toward AI regulation, arguing that excessive oversight could weaken competitiveness against China. He said on Tuesday that he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology. Clayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter. This is the second time Trump has named an adviser to oversee AI-related decisions across the administration. Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar role at the beginning of Trump's second term. The task force's vice chairs will be Emil Michael, Scott Kupor and Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, while members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, according to the report. External advisers will also include Sacks and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, the Journal said. passages: Tether relaunches its $184 billion USDT on Bitcoin in October 2026, 12 years after abandoning it for faster, cheaper networks like Tron and Ethereum.
This new integration will connect Bitcoin, the oldest blockchain, directly with USDT, the largest stablecoin valued at around $184 billion, designed to maintain a value of $1.
Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino captured the sentiment of this return with the phrase, "It's coming home." But does this move mean that Bitcoin will become a payments network again?
So far, Tether has not disclosed any exchanges or payment companies that plan to support the Bitcoin version.
El Salvador illustrates the struggle Bitcoin has faced as a payment method.
Although the country adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, a University of Central America survey revealed that 92% of Salvadorans reported not using it in 2024.
Recently, on September 29, the government announced plans for a stablecoin platform called Sivar on Coinbase's Base network, rather than building it on Bitcoin.
Additionally, El Salvador has opted for another blockchain for its stablecoin initiatives.
As a result, this relaunch primarily benefits Tether by reaching new users, while Bitcoin holders see minimal short-term change in BTC price or miner income.
This time, Utexo—a company backed by Tether with a license to distribute USDT under Tether's brand through exchanges, wallets, and payment providers —will issue USDT.
Bitcoin holders might find the launch less beneficial than it appears at first glance.

A USDT balance on Bitcoin represents a dollar claim on Tether, meaning it offers no exposure to Bitcoin's price fluctuations, and the limits and rules governing Bitcoin's 21 million coins remain unchanged.
As with XRP, increased network activity does not automatically increase demand for BTC.

This design enables private transfers, direct exchanges between BTC and USDT, and Bitcoin-backed loans without creating additional tokens.

passages: Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, Coinbase, and Shopify committed $1 billion to Open USD, launched September 30 against Tether's $184 billion market cap.
A stablecoin is designed to maintain a value of $1, and with major payment companies backing it, OUSD is entering the market with significant support.
The $1 billion represents liquidity that these partners are ready to provide, allowing users to easily convert OUSD into dollars.
While this commitment is substantial, it still pales in comparison to the existing market giants.
This raises the question: Does Open USD pose a threat to Tether (CRYPTO: USDT), USD Coin (CRYPTO: USDC), and Ripple's RLUSD (CRYPTO: RLUSD)?
The clearest sign of Open USD's impact will be how it is used for settlements.

If Visa, Mastercard, or Stripe start processing payments in OUSD by default, or if OUSD's supply grows into the tens of billions by mid-2027, the competitive landscape for all three established stablecoins could shift dramatically.
OUSD’s profit-sharing structure could incentivize Coinbase, Visa, and other partners to favor it over USDC, potentially pulling more business away from Circle.
OUSD is significantly smaller than established players.
Adding pressure is Visa's involvement; the company has been working on settlement programs using USDC, while it now supports a rival that shares its revenue.
So far, Visa, Mastercard, and Stripe have not committed to using OUSD for default merchant or card transactions, yet doing so could significantly boost its usage.
The company Bridge, acquired by Stripe for $1.1 billion in 2024, issues OUSD and provides monthly updates on its reserves.

passages: Tether is bringing its $184 billion stablecoin back to Bitcoin for the first time in over a decade, but the technology powering this comeback raises serious questions about whether Bitcoin holders and miners stand to gain anything at all.
Tether is set to relaunch its USDT ( CRYPTO: USDT ) stablecoin on the Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) network in October 2026, marking a return 12 years after its initial launch.
This new integration will connect Bitcoin, the oldest blockchain, directly with USDT, the largest stablecoin valued at around $184 billion, designed to maintain a value of $1.
In previous years, USDT shifted away from Bitcoin to take advantage of faster and cheaper networks, predominantly operating on platforms like Tron and Ethereum.
Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino captured the sentiment of this return with the phrase, “It’s coming home.” But does this move mean that Bitcoin will become a payments network again?
So far, Tether has not disclosed any exchanges or payment companies that plan to support the Bitcoin version.
El Salvador illustrates the struggle Bitcoin has faced as a payment method.
Although the country adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, a University of Central America survey revealed that 92% of Salvadorans reported not using it in 2024.
Recently, on September 29, the government announced plans for a stablecoin platform called Sivar on Coinbase’s Base network, rather than building it on Bitcoin.
Additionally, El Salvador has opted for another blockchain for its stablecoin initiatives.
As a result, this relaunch primarily benefits Tether by reaching new users, while Bitcoin holders see minimal short-term change in BTC price o r miner income .
This time, Utexo—a company backed by Tether with a license to distribute USDT under Tether’s brand through exchanges, wallets, and payment providers —will issue USDT.
Bitcoin holders might find the launch less beneficial than it appears at first glance.

A USDT balance on Bitcoin represents a dollar claim on Tether, meaning it offers no exposure to Bitcoin’s price fluctuations, and the limits and rules governing Bitcoin’s 21 million coins remain unchanged.
As with XRP , increased network activity does not automatically increase demand for BTC.
Tether provides regular updates on how much USDT it has issued on each network, making it easy to track progress.

If major exchanges begin to support Bitcoin-based USDT and its supply increases steadily through March 2027, particularly with Lightning support in place, Bitcoin could reclaim a portion of the payments landscape.
Utexo builds on the RGB protocol, which enables tokens to operate on Bitcoin while keeping most transaction details private off the public ledger.
This design enables private transfers, direct exchanges between BTC and USDT, and Bitcoin-backed loans without creating additional tokens.
Utexo also plans to integrate USDT into the Lightning Network, Bitcoin’s faster payment layer.
Furthermore, Bitcoin’s inherent design can hinder heavy payment traffic.

It adds a new block about every 10 minutes, which simplifies verification but limits the number of transactions it can process—leading to higher fees and longer wait times during periods of high demand.

Tether is set to relaunch its USDT ( CRYPTO: USDT ) stablecoin on the Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) network in October 2026, marking a return 12 years after its initial launch. This new integration will connect Bitcoin, the oldest blockchain, directly with USDT, the largest stablecoin valued at around $184 billion, designed to maintain a value of $1.

In previous years, USDT shifted away from Bitcoin to take advantage of faster and cheaper networks, predominantly operating on platforms like Tron and Ethereum. Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino captured the sentiment of this return with the phrase, “It’s coming home.” But does this move mean that Bitcoin will become a payments network again?

Tether originally launched USDT on Bitcoin in 2014 using the Omni protocol, which recorded tokens on the Bitcoin blockchain. This time, Utexo—a company backed by Tether with a license to distribute USDT under Tether’s brand through exchanges, wallets, and payment providers —will issue USDT.

Utexo builds on the RGB protocol, which enables tokens to operate on Bitcoin while keeping most transaction details private off the public ledger. This design enables private transfers, direct exchanges between BTC and USDT, and Bitcoin-backed loans without creating additional tokens. Utexo also plans to integrate USDT into the Lightning Network, Bitcoin’s faster payment layer.

Bitcoin holders might find the launch less beneficial than it appears at first glance. A USDT balance on Bitcoin represents a dollar claim on Tether, meaning it offers no exposure to Bitcoin’s price fluctuations, and the limits and rules governing Bitcoin’s 21 million coins remain unchanged. As with XRP , increased network activity does not automatically increase demand for BTC.

Miners may also earn less than expected. They generate new coins alongside transaction fees for recording each transaction. However, as the reward for mining new coins halves roughly every four years, fees need to pay for Bitcoin’s security over time. The RGB protocol keeps most transfer data off Bitcoin’s main chain, resulting in significantly lower fee revenue from USDT transactions than from full on-chain transfers.

The privacy aspect could spark more interest than potential fees. Researchers have already suggested integrating shielded Bitcoin using Zcash’s privacy technology, and private dollar transfers on Bitcoin could appeal to businesses that don’t want every transaction visible on a public ledger.

Competition poses a significant obstacle to Bitcoin’s resurgence as a payments network. For years, exchanges, wallets, and payment apps have handled USDT deposits and withdrawals primarily on Tron and Ethereum, where transfers are faster and cheaper. So far, Tether has not disclosed any exchanges or payment companies that plan to support the Bitcoin version.

Furthermore, Bitcoin’s inherent design can hinder heavy payment traffic. It adds a new block about every 10 minutes, which simplifies verification but limits the number of transactions it can process—leading to higher fees and longer wait times during periods of high demand. The Lightning Network was created to address this issue, so Utexo’s plan to add USDT to the Lightning Network will be crucial to its success.

El Salvador illustrates the struggle Bitcoin has faced as a payment method. Although the country adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, a University of Central America survey revealed that 92% of Salvadorans reported not using it in 2024. Recently, on September 29, the government announced plans for a stablecoin platform called Sivar on Coinbase’s Base network, rather than building it on Bitcoin.

Not with this launch alone. While USDT on Bitcoin offers a dollar-backed token for payments, private transfers, and swaps, Tron and Ethereum still hold most USDT. Additionally, El Salvador has opted for another blockchain for its stablecoin initiatives. As a result, this relaunch primarily benefits Tether by reaching new users, while Bitcoin holders see minimal short-term change in BTC price o r miner income .

Tether provides regular updates on how much USDT it has issued on each network, making it easy to track progress. If major exchanges begin to support Bitcoin-based USDT and its supply increases steadily through March 2027, particularly with Lightning support in place, Bitcoin could reclaim a portion of the payments landscape.

On the other hand, if USDT’s supply on Bitcoin remains relatively small compared to Tron and Ethereum, this relaunch might simply add another token to the mix without significantly increasing payment activity on Bitcoin.

Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, Coinbase, and Shopify committed $1 billion to Open USD, launched September 30 against Tether's $184 billion market cap.
A stablecoin is designed to maintain a value of $1, and with major payment companies backing it, OUSD is entering the market with significant support.
The $1 billion represents liquidity that these partners are ready to provide, allowing users to easily convert OUSD into dollars.
While this commitment is substantial, it still pales in comparison to the existing market giants.
This raises the question: Does Open USD pose a threat to Tether (CRYPTO: USDT), USD Coin (CRYPTO: USDC), and Ripple's RLUSD (CRYPTO: RLUSD)?
The clearest sign of Open USD's impact will be how it is used for settlements.

If Visa, Mastercard, or Stripe start processing payments in OUSD by default, or if OUSD's supply grows into the tens of billions by mid-2027, the competitive landscape for all three established stablecoins could shift dramatically.
OUSD’s profit-sharing structure could incentivize Coinbase, Visa, and other partners to favor it over USDC, potentially pulling more business away from Circle.
OUSD is significantly smaller than established players.
Adding pressure is Visa's involvement; the company has been working on settlement programs using USDC, while it now supports a rival that shares its revenue.
So far, Visa, Mastercard, and Stripe have not committed to using OUSD for default merchant or card transactions, yet doing so could significantly boost its usage.
The company Bridge, acquired by Stripe for $1.1 billion in 2024, issues OUSD and provides monthly updates on its reserves.
BlackRock, Lead Bank, and BNY Mellon manage these reserves.
The organization behind OUSD, Open Standard, reports that its partner network has grown to over 200 companies, up from 140 in June.
Ripple sells RLUSD to banks and payment institutions for cross-border transactions, just the type of customers that OUSD’s partners are already accommodating.
With OUSD backed by major players like Visa and Mastercard, institutions assessing payment networks will have to consider this strong competitor.
Among established tokens, USDC faces the biggest risk from Open USD.
Circle already splits reserve income with its distributors, and since Coinbase benefits from USDC revenue and is also an OUSD partner, it can promote whichever token offers them more profit.
Unlike Tether and Circle, which issue USDC and keep most of the interest income from their reserves, OUSD shares most of that revenue with its partners.
These partners receive earnings based on their participation, and they can create and redeem tokens at $1 without any fees.
This existing habit helped them establish extensive markets that a new entrant cannot replicate overnight.
However, OUSD is starting within the financial systems that handle payments directly, leveraging card networks and Shopify stores, where USDT and USDC have minimal influence.
This market includes many of the 35% of Americans who now own cryptocurrency.
As Open Standard CEO Zach Abrams explains, "Every other stablecoin is building a fund.

passages: Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, Coinbase, and Shopify committed $1 billion to Open USD, launched September 30 against Tether's $184 billion market cap.
A stablecoin is designed to maintain a value of $1, and with major payment companies backing it, OUSD is entering the market with significant support.
The $1 billion represents liquidity that these partners are ready to provide, allowing users to easily convert OUSD into dollars.
While this commitment is substantial, it still pales in comparison to the existing market giants.
This raises the question: Does Open USD pose a threat to Tether (CRYPTO: USDT), USD Coin (CRYPTO: USDC), and Ripple's RLUSD (CRYPTO: RLUSD)?
The clearest sign of Open USD's impact will be how it is used for settlements.

If Visa, Mastercard, or Stripe start processing payments in OUSD by default, or if OUSD's supply grows into the tens of billions by mid-2027, the competitive landscape for all three established stablecoins could shift dramatically.
OUSD’s profit-sharing structure could incentivize Coinbase, Visa, and other partners to favor it over USDC, potentially pulling more business away from Circle.
OUSD is significantly smaller than established players.
Adding pressure is Visa's involvement; the company has been working on settlement programs using USDC, while it now supports a rival that shares its revenue.
So far, Visa, Mastercard, and Stripe have not committed to using OUSD for default merchant or card transactions, yet doing so could significantly boost its usage.
The company Bridge, acquired by Stripe for $1.1 billion in 2024, issues OUSD and provides monthly updates on its reserves.
BlackRock, Lead Bank, and BNY Mellon manage these reserves.
The organization behind OUSD, Open Standard, reports that its partner network has grown to over 200 companies, up from 140 in June.
Ripple sells RLUSD to banks and payment institutions for cross-border transactions, just the type of customers that OUSD’s partners are already accommodating.
With OUSD backed by major players like Visa and Mastercard, institutions assessing payment networks will have to consider this strong competitor.
Among established tokens, USDC faces the biggest risk from Open USD.
Circle already splits reserve income with its distributors, and since Coinbase benefits from USDC revenue and is also an OUSD partner, it can promote whichever token offers them more profit.
Unlike Tether and Circle, which issue USDC and keep most of the interest income from their reserves, OUSD shares most of that revenue with its partners.
These partners receive earnings based on their participation, and they can create and redeem tokens at $1 without any fees.
This existing habit helped them establish extensive markets that a new entrant cannot replicate overnight.
However, OUSD is starting within the financial systems that handle payments directly, leveraging card networks and Shopify stores, where USDT and USDC have minimal influence.
This market includes many of the 35% of Americans who now own cryptocurrency.
As Open Standard CEO Zach Abrams explains, "Every other stablecoin is building a fund.
For XRP holders (CRYPTO:XRP), the fate of RLUSD primarily relates to Ripple's business developments and does not directly influence XRP’s value.

passages: Tether is bringing its $184 billion stablecoin back to Bitcoin for the first time in over a decade, but the technology powering this comeback raises serious questions about whether Bitcoin holders and miners stand to gain anything at all.
Tether is set to relaunch its USDT ( CRYPTO: USDT ) stablecoin on the Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) network in October 2026, marking a return 12 years after its initial launch.
This new integration will connect Bitcoin, the oldest blockchain, directly with USDT, the largest stablecoin valued at around $184 billion, designed to maintain a value of $1.
In previous years, USDT shifted away from Bitcoin to take advantage of faster and cheaper networks, predominantly operating on platforms like Tron and Ethereum.
Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino captured the sentiment of this return with the phrase, “It’s coming home.” But does this move mean that Bitcoin will become a payments network again?
So far, Tether has not disclosed any exchanges or payment companies that plan to support the Bitcoin version.
El Salvador illustrates the struggle Bitcoin has faced as a payment method.
Although the country adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, a University of Central America survey revealed that 92% of Salvadorans reported not using it in 2024.
Recently, on September 29, the government announced plans for a stablecoin platform called Sivar on Coinbase’s Base network, rather than building it on Bitcoin.
Additionally, El Salvador has opted for another blockchain for its stablecoin initiatives.
As a result, this relaunch primarily benefits Tether by reaching new users, while Bitcoin holders see minimal short-term change in BTC price o r miner income .
This time, Utexo—a company backed by Tether with a license to distribute USDT under Tether’s brand through exchanges, wallets, and payment providers —will issue USDT.
Bitcoin holders might find the launch less beneficial than it appears at first glance.

A USDT balance on Bitcoin represents a dollar claim on Tether, meaning it offers no exposure to Bitcoin’s price fluctuations, and the limits and rules governing Bitcoin’s 21 million coins remain unchanged.
As with XRP , increased network activity does not automatically increase demand for BTC.
Tether provides regular updates on how much USDT it has issued on each network, making it easy to track progress.

If major exchanges begin to support Bitcoin-based USDT and its supply increases steadily through March 2027, particularly with Lightning support in place, Bitcoin could reclaim a portion of the payments landscape.
Utexo builds on the RGB protocol, which enables tokens to operate on Bitcoin while keeping most transaction details private off the public ledger.
This design enables private transfers, direct exchanges between BTC and USDT, and Bitcoin-backed loans without creating additional tokens.
Utexo also plans to integrate USDT into the Lightning Network, Bitcoin’s faster payment layer.
Furthermore, Bitcoin’s inherent design can hinder heavy payment traffic.

It adds a new block about every 10 minutes, which simplifies verification but limits the number of transactions it can process—leading to higher fees and longer wait times during periods of high demand.

Tether is set to relaunch its USDT ( CRYPTO: USDT ) stablecoin on the Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) network in October 2026, marking a return 12 years after its initial launch. This new integration will connect Bitcoin, the oldest blockchain, directly with USDT, the largest stablecoin valued at around $184 billion, designed to maintain a value of $1.

In previous years, USDT shifted away from Bitcoin to take advantage of faster and cheaper networks, predominantly operating on platforms like Tron and Ethereum. Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino captured the sentiment of this return with the phrase, “It’s coming home.” But does this move mean that Bitcoin will become a payments network again?

Tether originally launched USDT on Bitcoin in 2014 using the Omni protocol, which recorded tokens on the Bitcoin blockchain. This time, Utexo—a company backed by Tether with a license to distribute USDT under Tether’s brand through exchanges, wallets, and payment providers —will issue USDT.

Utexo builds on the RGB protocol, which enables tokens to operate on Bitcoin while keeping most transaction details private off the public ledger. This design enables private transfers, direct exchanges between BTC and USDT, and Bitcoin-backed loans without creating additional tokens. Utexo also plans to integrate USDT into the Lightning Network, Bitcoin’s faster payment layer.

Bitcoin holders might find the launch less beneficial than it appears at first glance. A USDT balance on Bitcoin represents a dollar claim on Tether, meaning it offers no exposure to Bitcoin’s price fluctuations, and the limits and rules governing Bitcoin’s 21 million coins remain unchanged. As with XRP , increased network activity does not automatically increase demand for BTC.

Miners may also earn less than expected. They generate new coins alongside transaction fees for recording each transaction. However, as the reward for mining new coins halves roughly every four years, fees need to pay for Bitcoin’s security over time. The RGB protocol keeps most transfer data off Bitcoin’s main chain, resulting in significantly lower fee revenue from USDT transactions than from full on-chain transfers.

The privacy aspect could spark more interest than potential fees. Researchers have already suggested integrating shielded Bitcoin using Zcash’s privacy technology, and private dollar transfers on Bitcoin could appeal to businesses that don’t want every transaction visible on a public ledger.

Competition poses a significant obstacle to Bitcoin’s resurgence as a payments network. For years, exchanges, wallets, and payment apps have handled USDT deposits and withdrawals primarily on Tron and Ethereum, where transfers are faster and cheaper. So far, Tether has not disclosed any exchanges or payment companies that plan to support the Bitcoin version.

Furthermore, Bitcoin’s inherent design can hinder heavy payment traffic. It adds a new block about every 10 minutes, which simplifies verification but limits the number of transactions it can process—leading to higher fees and longer wait times during periods of high demand. The Lightning Network was created to address this issue, so Utexo’s plan to add USDT to the Lightning Network will be crucial to its success.

El Salvador illustrates the struggle Bitcoin has faced as a payment method. Although the country adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, a University of Central America survey revealed that 92% of Salvadorans reported not using it in 2024. Recently, on September 29, the government announced plans for a stablecoin platform called Sivar on Coinbase’s Base network, rather than building it on Bitcoin.

Not with this launch alone. While USDT on Bitcoin offers a dollar-backed token for payments, private transfers, and swaps, Tron and Ethereum still hold most USDT. Additionally, El Salvador has opted for another blockchain for its stablecoin initiatives. As a result, this relaunch primarily benefits Tether by reaching new users, while Bitcoin holders see minimal short-term change in BTC price o r miner income .

Tether provides regular updates on how much USDT it has issued on each network, making it easy to track progress. If major exchanges begin to support Bitcoin-based USDT and its supply increases steadily through March 2027, particularly with Lightning support in place, Bitcoin could reclaim a portion of the payments landscape.

On the other hand, if USDT’s supply on Bitcoin remains relatively small compared to Tron and Ethereum, this relaunch might simply add another token to the mix without significantly increasing payment activity on Bitcoin.

Jay Clayton will lead the force as DNI, serving as AI czar. Task force scope and deliverables (reporting/targets) . 10 of 12 outlets skipped it: SIF will review reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks, and jailbreaks . Independent highlights concrete deliverables; Washington Post foregrounds political anxiety response. President Donald Trump announced Sunday the creation of a "Super Intelligence Force" to coordinate federal initiatives aimed at maintaining US leadership in cutting-edge technology. Trump said the force would coordinate federal interactions with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers and commercial developers. Trump said the leadership team would include Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering and Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor. Trump said the group will report directly to him and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, and the task force will have 120 days to prepare its findings. Trump said the task force will examine existing laws and potential steps Congress could take while working with the technology industry to identify risks and opportunities. Jay Clayton said the task force's core mission is to ensure the United States continues to lead in the superintelligence race while putting the interests of the American people first. Clayton said, "The risk of not being first is very high," and he said that if the United States fails to maintain its lead, both known and unknown risks will rise. The executive order directed that the term "artificial intelligence" be replaced with "super intelligence," signaling the new administration's intent to redefine the strategic positioning of the technology. Trump said the heads of the largest US tech companies signed a "morally binding" agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence, including internal safety monitoring and independent external reviews of their systems. T Trump said the task force's charter calls for developing plans to respond to threats posed by advanced AI, while avoiding regulations that could hinder innovation and competition. The executive order named Emil Michael as responsible for coordinating with AI companies, Scott Kupor as responsible for liaising with critical infrastructure operators and other industry stakeholders, and Andrew Ferguson as responsible for consumer interests and issues related to religion, children, privacy, speech, and freedom of association. The task force members span the core decision-making circle of the Trump administration, including Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. The charter also directs the task force to review how breaches, hacks, model jailbreaks and other AI-related incidents are reported to the government, and recommend ways to improve the federal response under existing authorities. SIF will review reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks, and jailbreaks . Reported by Anadolu Ajansı and The Independent . Trump said the group will coordinate the federal government's engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers and AI companies. Trump said the force will work to safeguard public interests while advancing capabilities, and he emphasized maintaining US leadership in technology while favoring voluntary industry safeguards as opposed to tighter government regulation. SIF will review reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks, and jailbreaks . Reported by Anadolu Ajansı and The Independent .
