extraction.body: President Trump announced the creation of a Super Intelligence Force on Sunday following meetings with top AI company executives and the signing of voluntary safety standards. The “Super Intelligence Force” will be helmed by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, who has been named AI Czar. CNBC reports that President Trump revealed plans for a new government initiative called the Super Intelligence Force in a Sunday announcement on Truth Social, following last week’s meetings with leaders from the nation’s largest artificial intelligence companies. The formation comes amid increasing public pressure for regulatory oversight of AI technology. The announcement followed what Trump called the Historic White House Accord on Super Intelligence, a gathering where major technology companies acknowledged their obligations to American citizens. In his social media post, Trump wrote that he was “announcing the formation of the Super Intelligence Force (SIF),” explaining that the task force would work alongside federal agencies. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will head the Super Intelligence Force, a selection that aligns with previous reports indicating he was the likely choice for an AI oversight position. CBS News had reported days earlier that sources expected Clayton to receive the AI czar appointment. Trump named three additional leaders who will work alongside Clayton. Andrew Ferguson, chairman of the FTC, will participate in the leadership structure. Emil Michael, who serves as under secretary for research and engineering and chief technology officer at the Pentagon, will also hold a leadership role. Scott Kupor, director of the Office of Personnel Management, rounds out the leadership team. All four officials will report directly to President Trump and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. The announcement follows a White House meeting with executives from six major technology companies working in the AI space. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia and Elon Musk’s SpaceX all sent leadership representatives to the gathering. During that meeting, company leaders signed a set of voluntary safety standards aimed at governing AI development. Following the meeting, Trump indicated to reporters that he would announce an AI czar within three or four days. He characterized the voluntary standards as morally binding and expressed confidence in the industry’s ability to self-regulate. Trump stated he was seeing “tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police.” The accord signed by the technology leaders, which Trump shared on Truth Social, consists of a single page outlining specific commitments. The companies pledged to implement four layers of controls and audits designed to verify AI models are functioning as intended. These safeguards include internal company evaluations, audits conducted by external firms, and reviews performed by each company’s board of directors. Additionally, the tech executives agreed to establish regular meetings focused on developing standards and best practices to enhance the safety of AI systems. This ongoing collaboration aims to create industry-wide protocols for responsible AI development and deployment. AI giants simultaneously release powerful AI models and call for industry regulation, with China adding further complexity to the issue. David Sacks has pointed out that when AI titans like Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, and Elon Musk call for a slowdown, they are not doing so out of altruism, but with the motivation to capture the industry and exclude themselves from antitrust laws — a conflict that President Donald Trump and his new Super Intelligence Force recognize. Jay Clayton will lead the force as DNI, serving as AI czar. Task force scope and deliverables (reporting/targets) . 10 of 12 outlets skipped it: SIF will review reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks, and jailbreaks . Independent highlights concrete deliverables; Washington Post foregrounds political anxiety response. President Donald Trump announced Sunday the creation of a "Super Intelligence Force" to coordinate federal initiatives aimed at maintaining US leadership in cutting-edge technology. Trump said the force would coordinate federal interactions with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers and commercial developers. Trump said the leadership team would include Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering and Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael, and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor. Trump said the group will report directly to him and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, and the task force will have 120 days to prepare its findings. Trump said the task force will examine existing laws and potential steps Congress could take while working with the technology industry to identify risks and opportunities. Jay Clayton said the task force's core mission is to ensure the United States continues to lead in the superintelligence race while putting the interests of the American people first. Clayton said, "The risk of not being first is very high," and he said that if the United States fails to maintain its lead, both known and unknown risks will rise. The executive order directed that the term "artificial intelligence" be replaced with "super intelligence," signaling the new administration's intent to redefine the strategic positioning of the technology. Trump said the heads of the largest US tech companies signed a "morally binding" agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence, including internal safety monitoring and independent external reviews of their systems. T Trump said the task force's charter calls for developing plans to respond to threats posed by advanced AI, while avoiding regulations that could hinder innovation and competition. The executive order named Emil Michael as responsible for coordinating with AI companies, Scott Kupor as responsible for liaising with critical infrastructure operators and other industry stakeholders, and Andrew Ferguson as responsible for consumer interests and issues related to religion, children, privacy, speech, and freedom of association. The task force members span the core decision-making circle of the Trump administration, including Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. The charter also directs the task force to review how breaches, hacks, model jailbreaks and other AI-related incidents are reported to the government, and recommend ways to improve the federal response under existing authorities. SIF will review reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks, and jailbreaks . Reported by Anadolu Ajansı and The Independent . Trump said the group will coordinate the federal government's engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers and AI companies. Trump said the force will work to safeguard public interests while advancing capabilities, and he emphasized maintaining US leadership in technology while favoring voluntary industry safeguards as opposed to tighter government regulation. SIF will review reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks, and jailbreaks . Reported by Anadolu Ajansı and The Independent .

extraction.body: FIA Single-Seater Director Nikolas Tombazis explained why race control took several minutes before deciding on a new starting procedure following the software chaos that unfolded during the formation laps of the Bahrain Grand Prix . The start of the Bahrain Grand Prix was thrown into chaos when several drivers encountered software-related problems during the formation laps. Lewis Hamilton was among those affected, briefly coming to a halt after being unable to accelerate before eventually getting going again following a software reset. Max Verstappen and Charles Leclerc experienced a similar issue but managed to continue without stopping, while Esteban Ocon and Valtteri Bottas also came to a halt before eventually restarting. With several cars affected and the starting procedure disrupted, race control suspended the process and delayed the start while the situation was assessed. The cars were subsequently directed through the pit lane before returning to the circuit, with officials taking several minutes to determine how the Grand Prix could safely get under way and establish a new starting procedure. Speaking to GPblog and other media after the race, Tombazis explained that software bugs are not necessarily caused by overly complex systems and can sometimes simply result from an oversight. He acknowledged that the software had not been tested as extensively as the FIA would have liked, largely because of the limited amount of wet running this season, with a combination of circumstances ultimately triggering the problem. The issue emerged during the formation laps when several cars slowed dramatically, creating a concertina effect that left some drivers almost at a complete standstill. The software bug then prevented power from being redeployed, leaving some cars unable to accelerate again. Tombazis admitted that more testing would probably have allowed the FIA to identify the problem before the race. Once the issue became apparent, the FIA quickly identified what was happening and began working under significant time pressure on a software update. The update then had to be distributed to the teams and installed on the cars before the starting procedure could resume. "Bugs in software are not always caused by something being too difficult. There's sometimes an oversight. That's why software gets tested much more extensively. We didn't manage to test the software as extensively as we would have liked because it was, there's been very little wet running this year, and there was a bit of a combination of circumstances which caused this bug to kick in. "Basically, the formation laps, some cars went very slowly, almost came to a standstill. There was a bit of a concertina effect between cars, and some cars almost stopped completely. And that bug prevented the power to be redeployed and for the cars to start again. "I think if we had had a bit more testing, we probably would have managed to catch it in time and not have such a situation. Once the problem happened, our guys realised very quickly what was happening and had to work under a lot of time pressure for an update to the software which was issued to the teams and the teams had to install it on their cars. "All of that took about 20 minutes. It may have felt like five hours for spectators waiting a race and for everybody else, which is understandable and we are sorry about that. But I think it was quite a fast reaction given the problem." Finally, explaining what triggered the bug, Tombazis added: "In some sectors the full power is reduced, and the triggering factor was some cars reaching a very low speed. I don't know exactly what speed that was, but some cars reaching this very low speed somehow entered into a loop which meant they couldn't re-accelerate. And then it looked as if they came to a stop."

extraction.body: You may have heard about the “software bug” which caused the chaos that forced the start of Formula 1’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to be aborted, but what is the bug and how exactly did it cause so much drama? After torrential rain delayed the initial start by 40 minutes, a start attempt had to be abandoned after multiple cars either crawled around or ground to a halt on the formation laps. This meant the race was delayed for over 45 minutes and led to complaints from F1 drivers who described it as “horrible” and evidence that F1 has become “too complicated”. It emerged after the race that a software bug had triggered the chaos. There’s an alternative engine mode mandated for rain-affected running with a maximum 250kW deployment, compared to a maximum of 350kW in dry conditions. It’s similar to the now- banned engine trick deployed earlier in the year and exposed by shutdowns in practice at Suzuka earlier this year. As an emergency measure, the FIA released new software that removed the 250kW restraint in those sectors so there was some MGU-K power to allow them to circulate in those sections at low speeds. The FIA issued a statement after the race, saying: “On the formation lap ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit’s sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars. “As a result, the FIA technical department removed the energy limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release distributed to all competitors during the race delay caused by heavy rain, enabling teams to make the necessary changes to the power unit before the start of the race. “This issue had not been detected by the FIA or the teams during testing or during the laps to the grid. The FIA, together with the teams and power unit manufacturers, will undertake a full review of the issue." The FIA also took the unusual step of sending FIA single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis to the post-race media pen to explain the situation in detail. “We didn't manage to test the software as extensively as we would have liked, because there's been very little wet running this year,” Tombazis explained. “There was a bit of a combination of circumstances which caused this bug to kick in. “Once the problem happened, our guys realised very quickly what was happening, and had to work under a lot of time pressure for an update to the software, which was issued to the teams, and the teams had to install it on their cars. “So all of that took about 20 minutes. It may have felt like five hours for spectators waiting in a race, and for everybody else, which is understandable, and we are sorry about that. But I think it was quite a fast reaction given the problem.” This grand prix was the first proper in-weekend running for the 2026 cars in rain-affected conditions. There had been warnings from those tests about how tricky these cars would be in rain-affected conditions this year, but the slow-speed conditions of the Malaysia formation laps weren’t tested. “I think it was a combination of the speed, the very low speeds, that was far more low than you would normally do in such a test that caused it,” Tombazis said. “I don't believe those [Pirelli] tests were in any way representative of that situation in order to help us catch it in time. “They didn't get tested enough. Normally, software has to be tested far more in detail, and unfortunately, well, I don't know if it's unfortunate or not, but this year we've had, generally speaking, very good weather, and that has been the reason why it happened so late.” Asked if it was a mistake not to have anticipated it, he added: “Well, any bug is a product of a mistake. I don't know of any software that doesn't have bugs and updates. Your computer probably gets updated every three days, those are all bugs. “Of course, anticipating these things is what one hopes to do, but sometimes some very combination of events isn't properly anticipated and causes the problem.” Tombazis added: “Sometimes things fall through the net and people learn, and you do a better job next time.” The FIA resolved the situation by sending software to all of the teams to download and install on their power units before the race was properly started. The FIA’s on-site technical department quickly recognised the issue and wrote that code, a “cobbled-up, hurried solution”, by Tombazis’s own admission, so the race could get underway. “Just to be clear, the software is developed by the FIA in collaboration with the teams. It's part of the standard code that we have that is common to all the cars,” Tombazis said. “So, yes, we are the regulator and we have this responsibility, but this software is developed by the FIA, by the supplier of the standard ECU [Motion Applied], and by the team and the PU manufacturers, all in collaboration. “None of these people anticipated the problem. It's clearly FIA software. We obviously have a big role in it. We need to do better, but it's software that is developed collaboratively by all the Formula 1 industry.” The entire power unit software has been developed for the last three to four years, producing “a huge list of issues found by the teams” that prompted multiple updates before the 2026 season started - but this issue slipped through. “Fortunately, our guys understood the issue very, very quickly, and the update was done, I think, very competently," Tombazis said. The FIA and the teams will undertake a full debrief after the race and while they’re confident this specific issue won’t happen again, it can’t guarantee there won’t be further glitches with such complicated engines. “When you have electrical energy and combustion energy all working together, and obviously when you want to ensure that there's sporting fairness between the teams, that is complicated,” Tombazis said. “We would all like it to be simpler, but the fact is when you have as much electrical energy, it does make it more complicated. A very strange start was followed by a race full of curveballs in F1's 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. Tombazis added: “Sometimes things fall through the net and people learn, and you do a better job next time.”

The entire power unit software has been developed for the last three to four years, producing “a huge list of issues found by the teams” that prompted multiple updates before the 2026 season started - but this issue slipped through.
“Fortunately, our guys understood the issue very, very quickly, and the update was done, I think, very competently," Tombazis said.

The FIA and the teams will undertake a full debrief after the race and while they’re confident this specific issue won’t happen again, it can’t guarantee there won’t be further glitches with such complicated engines.

“When you have electrical energy and combustion energy all working together, and obviously when you want to ensure that there's sporting fairness between the teams, that is complicated,” Tombazis said.
“We would all like it to be simpler, but the fact is when you have as much electrical energy, it does make it more complicated.

extraction.body: FIA Single-Seater Director Nikolas Tombazis explained why race control took several minutes before deciding on a new starting procedure following the software chaos that unfolded during the formation laps of the Bahrain Grand Prix . The start of the Bahrain Grand Prix was thrown into chaos when several drivers encountered software-related problems during the formation laps. Lewis Hamilton was among those affected, briefly coming to a halt after being unable to accelerate before eventually getting going again following a software reset. Max Verstappen and Charles Leclerc experienced a similar issue but managed to continue without stopping, while Esteban Ocon and Valtteri Bottas also came to a halt before eventually restarting. With several cars affected and the starting procedure disrupted, race control suspended the process and delayed the start while the situation was assessed. The cars were subsequently directed through the pit lane before returning to the circuit, with officials taking several minutes to determine how the Grand Prix could safely get under way and establish a new starting procedure. Speaking to GPblog and other media after the race, Tombazis explained that software bugs are not necessarily caused by overly complex systems and can sometimes simply result from an oversight. He acknowledged that the software had not been tested as extensively as the FIA would have liked, largely because of the limited amount of wet running this season, with a combination of circumstances ultimately triggering the problem. The issue emerged during the formation laps when several cars slowed dramatically, creating a concertina effect that left some drivers almost at a complete standstill. The software bug then prevented power from being redeployed, leaving some cars unable to accelerate again. Tombazis admitted that more testing would probably have allowed the FIA to identify the problem before the race. Once the issue became apparent, the FIA quickly identified what was happening and began working under significant time pressure on a software update. The update then had to be distributed to the teams and installed on the cars before the starting procedure could resume. "Bugs in software are not always caused by something being too difficult. There's sometimes an oversight. That's why software gets tested much more extensively. We didn't manage to test the software as extensively as we would have liked because it was, there's been very little wet running this year, and there was a bit of a combination of circumstances which caused this bug to kick in. "Basically, the formation laps, some cars went very slowly, almost came to a standstill. There was a bit of a concertina effect between cars, and some cars almost stopped completely. And that bug prevented the power to be redeployed and for the cars to start again. "I think if we had had a bit more testing, we probably would have managed to catch it in time and not have such a situation. Once the problem happened, our guys realised very quickly what was happening and had to work under a lot of time pressure for an update to the software which was issued to the teams and the teams had to install it on their cars. "All of that took about 20 minutes. It may have felt like five hours for spectators waiting a race and for everybody else, which is understandable and we are sorry about that. But I think it was quite a fast reaction given the problem." Finally, explaining what triggered the bug, Tombazis added: "In some sectors the full power is reduced, and the triggering factor was some cars reaching a very low speed. I don't know exactly what speed that was, but some cars reaching this very low speed somehow entered into a loop which meant they couldn't re-accelerate. And then it looked as if they came to a stop."

After torrential rain delayed the initial start by 40 minutes, a start attempt had to be abandoned after multiple cars either crawled around or ground to a halt on the formation laps. It emerged after the race that a software bug had triggered the chaos. There’s an alternative engine mode mandated for rain-affected running with a maximum 250kW deployment, compared to a maximum of 350kW in dry conditions. It’s similar to the now- banned engine trick deployed earlier in the year and exposed by shutdowns in practice at Suzuka earlier this year. As an emergency measure, the FIA released new software that removed the 250kW restraint in those sectors so there was some MGU-K power to allow them to circulate in those sections at low speeds. The FIA issued a statement after the race, saying: “On the formation lap ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit’s sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars. “As a result, the FIA technical department removed the energy limit constraint in the affected sectors through an updated software release distributed to all competitors during the race delay caused by heavy rain, enabling teams to make the necessary changes to the power unit before the start of the race. “This issue had not been detected by the FIA or the teams during testing or during the laps to the grid. “They didn't get tested enough. Normally, software has to be tested far more in detail, and unfortunately, well, I don't know if it's unfortunate or not, but this year we've had, generally speaking, very good weather, and that has been the reason why it happened so late.”

Asked if it was a mistake not to have anticipated it, he added: “Well, any bug is a product of a mistake. I don't know of any software that doesn't have bugs and updates. Your computer probably gets updated every three days, those are all bugs.
“Of course, anticipating these things is what one hopes to do, but sometimes some very combination of events isn't properly anticipated and causes the problem.”
Tombazis added: “Sometimes things fall through the net and people learn, and you do a better job next time.”
The FIA resolved the situation by sending software to all of the teams to download and install on their power units before the race was properly started.
The FIA’s on-site technical department quickly recognised the issue and wrote that code, a “cobbled-up, hurried solution”, by Tombazis’s own admission, so the race could get underway.
“Just to be clear, the software is developed by the FIA in collaboration with the teams. It's part of the standard code that we have that is common to all the cars,” Tombazis said.

“So, yes, we are the regulator and we have this responsibility, but this software is developed by the FIA, by the supplier of the standard ECU [Motion Applied], and by the team and the PU manufacturers, all in collaboration.

“None of these people anticipated the problem. It's clearly FIA software. We obviously have a big role in it. We need to do better, but it's software that is developed collaboratively by all the Formula 1 industry.”

The entire power unit software has been developed for the last three to four years, producing “a huge list of issues found by the teams” that prompted multiple updates before the 2026 season started - but this issue slipped through.
“Fortunately, our guys understood the issue very, very quickly, and the update was done, I think, very competently," Tombazis said.

The FIA and the teams will undertake a full debrief after the race and while they’re confident this specific issue won’t happen again, it can’t guarantee there won’t be further glitches with such complicated engines.

“When you have electrical energy and combustion energy all working together, and obviously when you want to ensure that there's sporting fairness between the teams, that is complicated,” Tombazis said.
“We would all like it to be simpler, but the fact is when you have as much electrical energy, it does make it more complicated.

sources.title: Trump taps Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as AI czar - CNBC
passages: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton was chosen as the Trump administration's new AI czar, leading its response to artificial intelligence amid growing concerns about the risks of this rapidly evolving technology.

In addition to Clayton, the task force will include: Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson; the Defense Department's Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering and Chief Technology Officer, Emil Michael; and Scott Kupor, director of the Office of Personnel Management.
"We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry.
Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump said the post, which also announced plans to hire an AI czar.
Venture capitalist David Sacks had previously served as AI and crypto czar under Trump, but in March said that his time as a special government employee had ended.

"The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump said in a Truth Social post Sunday.
The announcement comes days after AI industry leaders met with Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson at the White House .
The AI developers signed onto an agreement of voluntary safety standards that Trump said was "morally binding."

Despite dire warnings from within the industry and calls from AI leaders Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for federal guardrails on frontier AI models, Trump has so far opposed regulation.
In the same September post, Trump suggested AI fears were a hoax and blamed "Radical Left Dumocrats."

passages: Tether relaunches its $184 billion USDT on Bitcoin in October 2026, 12 years after abandoning it for faster, cheaper networks like Tron and Ethereum.
This new integration will connect Bitcoin, the oldest blockchain, directly with USDT, the largest stablecoin valued at around $184 billion, designed to maintain a value of $1.
Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino captured the sentiment of this return with the phrase, "It's coming home." But does this move mean that Bitcoin will become a payments network again?
So far, Tether has not disclosed any exchanges or payment companies that plan to support the Bitcoin version.
El Salvador illustrates the struggle Bitcoin has faced as a payment method.
Although the country adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, a University of Central America survey revealed that 92% of Salvadorans reported not using it in 2024.
Recently, on September 29, the government announced plans for a stablecoin platform called Sivar on Coinbase's Base network, rather than building it on Bitcoin.
Additionally, El Salvador has opted for another blockchain for its stablecoin initiatives.
As a result, this relaunch primarily benefits Tether by reaching new users, while Bitcoin holders see minimal short-term change in BTC price or miner income.
This time, Utexo—a company backed by Tether with a license to distribute USDT under Tether's brand through exchanges, wallets, and payment providers —will issue USDT.
Bitcoin holders might find the launch less beneficial than it appears at first glance.

A USDT balance on Bitcoin represents a dollar claim on Tether, meaning it offers no exposure to Bitcoin's price fluctuations, and the limits and rules governing Bitcoin's 21 million coins remain unchanged.
As with XRP, increased network activity does not automatically increase demand for BTC.
Tether provides regular updates on how much USDT it has issued on each network, making it easy to track progress.

This design enables private transfers, direct exchanges between BTC and USDT, and Bitcoin-backed loans without creating additional tokens.

Tether is set to relaunch its USDT ( CRYPTO: USDT ) stablecoin on the Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) network in October 2026, marking a return 12 years after its initial launch. This new integration will connect Bitcoin, the oldest blockchain, directly with USDT, the largest stablecoin valued at around $184 billion, designed to maintain a value of $1.

In previous years, USDT shifted away from Bitcoin to take advantage of faster and cheaper networks, predominantly operating on platforms like Tron and Ethereum. Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino captured the sentiment of this return with the phrase, “It’s coming home.” But does this move mean that Bitcoin will become a payments network again?

Tether originally launched USDT on Bitcoin in 2014 using the Omni protocol, which recorded tokens on the Bitcoin blockchain. This time, Utexo—a company backed by Tether with a license to distribute USDT under Tether’s brand through exchanges, wallets, and payment providers —will issue USDT.

Utexo builds on the RGB protocol, which enables tokens to operate on Bitcoin while keeping most transaction details private off the public ledger. This design enables private transfers, direct exchanges between BTC and USDT, and Bitcoin-backed loans without creating additional tokens. Utexo also plans to integrate USDT into the Lightning Network, Bitcoin’s faster payment layer.

Bitcoin holders might find the launch less beneficial than it appears at first glance. A USDT balance on Bitcoin represents a dollar claim on Tether, meaning it offers no exposure to Bitcoin’s price fluctuations, and the limits and rules governing Bitcoin’s 21 million coins remain unchanged. As with XRP , increased network activity does not automatically increase demand for BTC.

Miners may also earn less than expected. They generate new coins alongside transaction fees for recording each transaction. However, as the reward for mining new coins halves roughly every four years, fees need to pay for Bitcoin’s security over time. The RGB protocol keeps most transfer data off Bitcoin’s main chain, resulting in significantly lower fee revenue from USDT transactions than from full on-chain transfers.

The privacy aspect could spark more interest than potential fees. Researchers have already suggested integrating shielded Bitcoin using Zcash’s privacy technology, and private dollar transfers on Bitcoin could appeal to businesses that don’t want every transaction visible on a public ledger.

Competition poses a significant obstacle to Bitcoin’s resurgence as a payments network. For years, exchanges, wallets, and payment apps have handled USDT deposits and withdrawals primarily on Tron and Ethereum, where transfers are faster and cheaper. So far, Tether has not disclosed any exchanges or payment companies that plan to support the Bitcoin version.

Furthermore, Bitcoin’s inherent design can hinder heavy payment traffic. It adds a new block about every 10 minutes, which simplifies verification but limits the number of transactions it can process—leading to higher fees and longer wait times during periods of high demand. The Lightning Network was created to address this issue, so Utexo’s plan to add USDT to the Lightning Network will be crucial to its success.

El Salvador illustrates the struggle Bitcoin has faced as a payment method. Although the country adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, a University of Central America survey revealed that 92% of Salvadorans reported not using it in 2024. Recently, on September 29, the government announced plans for a stablecoin platform called Sivar on Coinbase’s Base network, rather than building it on Bitcoin.

Not with this launch alone. While USDT on Bitcoin offers a dollar-backed token for payments, private transfers, and swaps, Tron and Ethereum still hold most USDT. Additionally, El Salvador has opted for another blockchain for its stablecoin initiatives. As a result, this relaunch primarily benefits Tether by reaching new users, while Bitcoin holders see minimal short-term change in BTC price o r miner income .

Tether provides regular updates on how much USDT it has issued on each network, making it easy to track progress. If major exchanges begin to support Bitcoin-based USDT and its supply increases steadily through March 2027, particularly with Lightning support in place, Bitcoin could reclaim a portion of the payments landscape.

On the other hand, if USDT’s supply on Bitcoin remains relatively small compared to Tron and Ethereum, this relaunch might simply add another token to the mix without significantly increasing payment activity on Bitcoin.

Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino captured the sentiment of this return with the phrase, "It's coming home." But does this move mean that Bitcoin will become a payments network again?
So far, Tether has not disclosed any exchanges or payment companies that plan to support the Bitcoin version.
El Salvador illustrates the struggle Bitcoin has faced as a payment method.
Although the country adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, a University of Central America survey revealed that 92% of Salvadorans reported not using it in 2024.
Recently, on September 29, the government announced plans for a stablecoin platform called Sivar on Coinbase's Base network, rather than building it on Bitcoin.
Additionally, El Salvador has opted for another blockchain for its stablecoin initiatives.
As a result, this relaunch primarily benefits Tether by reaching new users, while Bitcoin holders see minimal short-term change in BTC price or miner income.
This time, Utexo—a company backed by Tether with a license to distribute USDT under Tether's brand through exchanges, wallets, and payment providers —will issue USDT.
Bitcoin holders might find the launch less beneficial than it appears at first glance.

A USDT balance on Bitcoin represents a dollar claim on Tether, meaning it offers no exposure to Bitcoin's price fluctuations, and the limits and rules governing Bitcoin's 21 million coins remain unchanged.
As with XRP, increased network activity does not automatically increase demand for BTC.
Tether provides regular updates on how much USDT it has issued on each network, making it easy to track progress.

If major exchanges begin to support Bitcoin-based USDT and its supply increases steadily through March 2027, particularly with Lightning support in place, Bitcoin could reclaim a portion of the payments landscape.
Utexo builds on the RGB protocol, which enables tokens to operate on Bitcoin while keeping most transaction details private off the public ledger.
This design enables private transfers, direct exchanges between BTC and USDT, and Bitcoin-backed loans without creating additional tokens.
Utexo also plans to integrate USDT into the Lightning Network, Bitcoin's faster payment layer.

Furthermore, Bitcoin's inherent design can hinder heavy payment traffic.

It adds a new block about every 10 minutes, which simplifies verification but limits the number of transactions it can process—leading to higher fees and longer wait times during periods of high demand.
They generate new coins alongside transaction fees for recording each transaction.
However, as the reward for mining new coins halves roughly every four years, fees need to pay for Bitcoin's security over time.
The privacy aspect could spark more interest than potential fees.

relevantPassages.text: Tether is bringing its $184 billion stablecoin back to Bitcoin for the first time in over a decade, but the technology powering this comeback raises serious questions about whether Bitcoin holders and miners stand to gain anything at all.
Tether is set to relaunch its USDT ( CRYPTO: USDT ) stablecoin on the Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) network in October 2026, marking a return 12 years after its initial launch.
This new integration will connect Bitcoin, the oldest blockchain, directly with USDT, the largest stablecoin valued at around $184 billion, designed to maintain a value of $1.
In previous years, USDT shifted away from Bitcoin to take advantage of faster and cheaper networks, predominantly operating on platforms like Tron and Ethereum.
Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino captured the sentiment of this return with the phrase, “It’s coming home.” But does this move mean that Bitcoin will become a payments network again?
So far, Tether has not disclosed any exchanges or payment companies that plan to support the Bitcoin version.
El Salvador illustrates the struggle Bitcoin has faced as a payment method.
Although the country adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, a University of Central America survey revealed that 92% of Salvadorans reported not using it in 2024.
Recently, on September 29, the government announced plans for a stablecoin platform called Sivar on Coinbase’s Base network, rather than building it on Bitcoin.
Additionally, El Salvador has opted for another blockchain for its stablecoin initiatives.
As a result, this relaunch primarily benefits Tether by reaching new users, while Bitcoin holders see minimal short-term change in BTC price o r miner income .
This time, Utexo—a company backed by Tether with a license to distribute USDT under Tether’s brand through exchanges, wallets, and payment providers —will issue USDT.
Bitcoin holders might find the launch less beneficial than it appears at first glance.

A USDT balance on Bitcoin represents a dollar claim on Tether, meaning it offers no exposure to Bitcoin’s price fluctuations, and the limits and rules governing Bitcoin’s 21 million coins remain unchanged.
As with XRP , increased network activity does not automatically increase demand for BTC.
Tether provides regular updates on how much USDT it has issued on each network, making it easy to track progress.

If major exchanges begin to support Bitcoin-based USDT and its supply increases steadily through March 2027, particularly with Lightning support in place, Bitcoin could reclaim a portion of the payments landscape.
Utexo builds on the RGB protocol, which enables tokens to operate on Bitcoin while keeping most transaction details private off the public ledger.
This design enables private transfers, direct exchanges between BTC and USDT, and Bitcoin-backed loans without creating additional tokens.
Utexo also plans to integrate USDT into the Lightning Network, Bitcoin’s faster payment layer.
Furthermore, Bitcoin’s inherent design can hinder heavy payment traffic.

It adds a new block about every 10 minutes, which simplifies verification but limits the number of transactions it can process—leading to higher fees and longer wait times during periods of high demand.

They forced a couple to transfer their cryptocurrency while injuring the husband and threatening his pregnant wife with a knife.
This shocking event underscores the importance of keeping crypto holdings private and securing both your identity and your keys.

Owning a cryptocurrency wallet is like keeping cash in a drawer; whoever holds the private keys—the secret codes needed to approve transactions—controls the coins.
Another critical decision for crypto holders is who controls the keys.
So as balances grow, how much should a household keep in self-custody to keep crypto private and its members safe?
Bitcoin's public blockchain makes crypto pseudonymous, not anonymous; one link between a wallet address and real identity exposes your full balance to thieves.

The couple, who were expecting their third child, were attacked after returning home at around 5.20pm on Saturday 13 December last year. As they opened their front door, three men got out of a car parked nearby and forced their way into the house behind them. In what police believe may have been a planned and targeted attack, the men demanded that the couple transfer cryptocurrency, with instructions relayed by a fourth offender on a video call. Describing how he was beaten during a 45-minute ordeal, the man told the BBC one offender put a pillow over his wife’s face, adding: “He’s literally suffocating her on the sofa. I can hear her screaming: ‘I can’t breathe.'” He said of the man communicating with the robbers on a video-call: “I can hear the guy on FaceTime saying: ‘Show me everything on his phone. Show me what apps he’s got.’ “He was basically saying: ‘Look, if you don’t send us this money now, we’re going to stab your wife in the stomach and kill your baby. All are attackers are thought to be their twenties, with one described as a black man with a small diagonal scar beneath his left eyebrow. West Midlands Police is investigating the robbery and has said the female victim was also threatened with a knife. Crimestoppers is offering a reward of up to £10,000 for information given exclusively to the charity that leads to the arrest and conviction of those responsible. Information can be passed to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111 or through its website. That’s precisely why our charity exists. We are not the police. We never ask for your name, we can’t trace your IP address, and you will never be asked to give a statement or go to court. In nearly 40 years we have never broken that promise. “If this has been sitting with you, please pass it on to us to help keep our communities safe. You can help this family without ever saying who you are.”

A hammer-wielding masked gang forced a man to transfer hundreds of thousands of pounds in cryptocurrency after threatening to kill his pregnant wife. Crimestoppers put up a £10,000 reward last month after the young couple, who do not wish to be identified, were attacked in their home in the Smith’s Wood area of Solihull , West Midlands . The couple, who were expecting their third child, were attacked after returning home at around 5.20pm on Saturday 13 December last year. As they opened their front door, three men got out of a car parked nearby and forced their way into the house behind them. In what police believe may have been a planned and targeted attack, the men demanded that the couple transfer cryptocurrency, with instructions relayed by a fourth offender on a video call. Describing how he was beaten during a 45-minute ordeal, the man told the BBC one offender put a pillow over his wife’s face, adding: “He’s literally suffocating her on the sofa. I can hear her screaming: ‘I can’t breathe.'” He said of the man communicating with the robbers on a video-call: “I can hear the guy on FaceTime saying: ‘Show me everything on his phone. Show me what apps he’s got.’ “He was basically saying: ‘Look, if you don’t send us this money now, we’re going to stab your wife in the stomach and kill your baby. We’re going to kill your wife.'” Several Rolex watches were also taken from the home of the victim, who told BBC he was an amateur investor in crypto coins who made enough money to quit his job in 2023 to trade full time. “They threatened my wife and my baby,” the man, who suffered significant injuries, added. “People need to understand these risks are real.” In a statement issued late last month alongside CCTV of the attackers entering the property, Crimestoppers said the offenders left the area in a car believed to be a black BMW X3. All are attackers are thought to be their twenties, with one described as a black man with a small diagonal scar beneath his left eyebrow. West Midlands Police is investigating the robbery and has said the female victim was also threatened with a knife. Crimestoppers is offering a reward of up to £10,000 for information given exclusively to the charity that leads to the arrest and conviction of those responsible. Information can be passed to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111 or through its website. Alan Edwards, Crimestoppers’ West Midlands regional manager, said: “This was a young family, at home, weeks away from welcoming a new baby. “We understand that speaking up about something like this feels daunting. That’s precisely why our charity exists. We are not the police. We never ask for your name, we can’t trace your IP address, and you will never be asked to give a statement or go to court. In nearly 40 years we have never broken that promise. “If this has been sitting with you, please pass it on to us to help keep our communities safe. You can help this family without ever saying who you are.”

passages: In our latest analysis, we asked AI models—ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini— to evaluate which cryptocurrency among Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH), and XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) is likely to bounce back to its all-time high first.
All three models gave the same ranking: Bitcoin led, followed by Ethereum, with XRP trailing.
ChatGPT predicts Bitcoin could close 2026 around $100,000, Ethereum at approximately $3,400, and XRP near $2.05.
Similarly, Gemini projects year-end prices of $108,500, $3,450, and $2.15, respectively.
ChatGPT assigned XRP only a 15% probability, while Gemini placed it at just 8%.
It has the smallest gap to cover, the largest amount of invested funds, and the smallest decline over the past year—down about 30%, compared with Ethereum's 38% and XRP's 50% drops.
The immediate critical test for Bitcoin is to surpass its recent high of $87,500, followed by the significant threshold of $100,000.
If Bitcoin falls below $80,000, it could hinder its progress and allow Ethereum to narrow its gap further.
If Ethereum exceeds $4,946 before Bitcoin returns to $126,080, it would suggest the AI models may have miscalculated the recovery order.
Grok noted that U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which hold Bitcoin and trade similarly to shares, have approximately $108 billion in assets.
In comparison, Ethereum funds have $17.8 billion, and XRP funds only $1.8 billion.
Grok mentioned that these funds hold nearly 6% of Bitcoin's total supply.
While the models agreed on the order, they differed in confidence.
This raises an interesting question: how much should we rely on these AI predictions when all three cryptocurrencies remain significantly below their previous peaks?
To reach their former highs, Bitcoin needs a gain of about 49%, Ethereum requires around 83%, and XRP must climb approximately 145%.
As a result, the ranking aligns almost perfectly with the size of the gap each cryptocurrency must close.
In terms of recent performance, Ethereum has shown more significant growth.
This shows Ethereum is closing the gap faster than Bitcoin and XRP.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Even optimistic year-end forecasts put Bitcoin near $100,000, which would still leave it about 21% short of its $126,080 record, with full recovery potentially extending into mid-2027.
Additionally, Gemini noted that new XRP supplies entering the market might dilute demand per token.
ChatGPT pointed out that Evernorth's 473 million XRP represents only a small fraction of XRP's $95 billion market value.
Grok observed that XRP's previous record in 2025 was more of a fleeting spike than a sustainable price level.

coreFacts.text: In our latest analysis, we asked AI models—ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini— to evaluate which cryptocurrency among Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH), and XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) is likely to bounce back to its all-time high first.
All three models gave the same ranking: Bitcoin led, followed by Ethereum, with XRP trailing.
ChatGPT predicts Bitcoin could close 2026 around $100,000, Ethereum at approximately $3,400, and XRP near $2.05.
Similarly, Gemini projects year-end prices of $108,500, $3,450, and $2.15, respectively.
ChatGPT assigned XRP only a 15% probability, while Gemini placed it at just 8%.
It has the smallest gap to cover, the largest amount of invested funds, and the smallest decline over the past year—down about 30%, compared with Ethereum's 38% and XRP's 50% drops.
The immediate critical test for Bitcoin is to surpass its recent high of $87,500, followed by the significant threshold of $100,000.
If Bitcoin falls below $80,000, it could hinder its progress and allow Ethereum to narrow its gap further.
If Ethereum exceeds $4,946 before Bitcoin returns to $126,080, it would suggest the AI models may have miscalculated the recovery order.
Grok noted that U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which hold Bitcoin and trade similarly to shares, have approximately $108 billion in assets.
In comparison, Ethereum funds have $17.8 billion, and XRP funds only $1.8 billion.
Grok mentioned that these funds hold nearly 6% of Bitcoin's total supply.
While the models agreed on the order, they differed in confidence.
This raises an interesting question: how much should we rely on these AI predictions when all three cryptocurrencies remain significantly below their previous peaks?
To reach their former highs, Bitcoin needs a gain of about 49%, Ethereum requires around 83%, and XRP must climb approximately 145%.
As a result, the ranking aligns almost perfectly with the size of the gap each cryptocurrency must close.
In terms of recent performance, Ethereum has shown more significant growth.
This shows Ethereum is closing the gap faster than Bitcoin and XRP.

While the models agreed on the order, they differed in confidence. ChatGPT estimated a 55% chance of Bitcoin reaching its record high first; Grok was slightly more optimistic at 58%, and Gemini was the most confident, giving Bitcoin a 70% probability. This raises an interesting question: how much should we rely on these AI predictions when all three cryptocurrencies remain significantly below their previous peaks?

Starting from their respective previous highs—$126,080 for Bitcoin, $4,946 for Ethereum , and $3.65 for XRP—we looked at the market as of October 1, 2026. At that time, Bitcoin was trading around $84,670, Ethereum at $2,699, and XRP at $1.49.

To reach their former highs, Bitcoin needs a gain of about 49%, Ethereum requires around 83%, and XRP must climb approximately 145%. As a result, the ranking aligns almost perfectly with the size of the gap each cryptocurrency must close.
Gemini highlighted the specific dollar amount Bitcoin needs to regain its past glory, saying it would require about $820 billion in market value to reach $126,080.

In terms of recent performance, Ethereum has shown more significant growth. Over the 90 days leading up to October 1, Ethereum climbed about 53%, while Bitcoin gained around 33% and XRP only 31%. This shows Ethereum is closing the gap faster than Bitcoin and XRP.

Despite this momentum, the AI models still favored Bitcoin. Grok noted that U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which hold Bitcoin and trade similarly to shares, have approximately $108 billion in assets. In comparison, Ethereum funds have $17.8 billion, and XRP funds only $1.8 billion. Grok mentioned that these funds hold nearly 6% of Bitcoin’s total supply.

Although XRP shows the highest percentage gain potential—ranging from 38% to 44%—its chances of being the first to reach its all-time high are quite low. ChatGPT assigned XRP only a 15% probability, while Gemini placed it at just 8%.
This skepticism about XRP stems from the fact that even a 40% increase over three months would still leave it far short of its high at $3.65, requiring a 145% surge.

Additionally, Gemini noted that new XRP supplies entering the market might dilute demand per token. ChatGPT pointed out that Evernorth’s 473 million XRP represents only a small fraction of XRP’s $95 billion market value. Grok observed that XRP’s previous record in 2025 was more of a fleeting spike than a sustainable price level.

extraction.body: Aviation security protocols under scrutiny after co-pilot accused of attempted axe attack aboard Flydubai flight. A Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking his captain with an emergency axe and attempting to seize control of the flight bound for Israel had previously been barred from flying over concerns about alleged “extremist” views, raising questions about how he was allowed to fly to Tel Aviv. The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national, according to multiple media reports. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has described the September 30 incident aboard Flight FZ1073 as an attempted “terrorist” operation . But investigators are still working to establish the motive and whether anyone else was connected to the attack, which has raised concerns about pilot vetting and aviation security. So, what security checks do pilots have to go through and how al-Hammami may have evaded background checks? That is now one of the central questions facing investigators. Al-Hammami had previously been barred from flying in Oman because of concerns that he had adopted “extremist” views and was instead moved to an administrative role at Oman Air, according to sources who spoke to the AP news agency. A Gulf diplomat told AP that al-Hammami had undergone standard security checks before being hired. It wasn’t immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted. The US-based network CNN reported that a LinkedIn profile bearing al-Hammami’s name said he had spent seven years at Oman Air before leaving in February 2025. The profile said he joined Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and left in January this year. It is unclear what those alleged views were or whether Oman informed other countries or airlines about its concerns. Background checks for commercial pilots vary by airline and country, with no single global standard governing the process, an airline pilot and instructor told Al Jazeera. The captain with an international airline who chose to remain anonymous said pilots are generally required to obtain aviation medical certification from the regulator in the country where they are licensed to fly. In the UAE, that is overseen by the General Civil Aviation Authority (GCAA), he said. Some airlines also require prospective pilots to provide police clearance certificates from their country of residence as part of pre-employment screening, the pilot added. One type of check is a Class 1 medical assessment, which typically examines areas including vision, hearing, cardiovascular and neurological health, as well as conditions that could cause sudden incapacitation. When it comes to security checks, aviation rules require background checks for personnel who have unescorted access to security-restricted areas. Psychological assessments, drug and alcohol testing and other evaluations may be required depending on the jurisdiction. Israel has some of the world’s toughest aviation security measures. As a result, questions have been raised over how the alleged attacker was allowed to operate a flight to Israel, despite reportedly being an Omani national and Oman having no diplomatic relations with Israel. According to the Haaretz newspaper, Israeli authorities received the Flydubai flight’s crew and passenger lists before it departed. Under a law passed in 2023, airlines are required to provide information about passengers and crew members, including their names and nationalities, to Israel up to 48 hours before a flight. The Israel Tax Authority confirmed to Haaretz that it had received the lists for the Flydubai flight. The media outlet reported that the information is also supposed to be available to Israeli security bodies, including the Mossad, police and Shin Bet, to identify people who may pose a security risk. According to security sources who spoke to Haaretz, the Transportation Ministry’s Security Department and the Mossad are responsible for checking foreign flight crews and issuing alerts if concerns arise. However, two security sources told Haaretz that while the Transportation Ministry holds responsibility “on paper”, it does not have its own intelligence capacity. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that Israel has longstanding arrangements with foreign airlines aimed at preventing pilots who are nationals of countries without diplomatic relations with Israel from flying there. Netanyahu has described what happened as a “loophole” and Israel says it will now strengthen its checks. The UAE has not yet publicly established a motive or announced whether investigators believe al-Hammami acted alone. UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said on Saturday that the latest ‘terrorist’ attack is a new warning that the region’s fight against “extremism” is not over. “This underscores the importance of the UAE’s early and firm stance: no tolerance for extremism and no leniency towards its rhetoric. Security begins with confronting hatred and drying up the sources of extremism,” he posted on X.

extraction.body: A security guard is wanted by Philadelphia police after shooting a man during a confrontation outside a club on the 1000 block of Spring Garden Street early Sunday. The 39-year-old victim was taken to Jefferson Hospital and is listed in stable condition, while the guard fled the scene before officers could make an arrest. According to 6abc , the confrontation began around 12:30 a.m. when a man and a woman got into an argument with the security guard outside the club. Investigators say the guard pulled out a gun and shot the man before running from the scene. Police have not released the guard's identity, and the search for the suspect remains active. The shooting adds to a string of recent incidents in which armed security personnel have used lethal force during confrontations at Philadelphia bars, clubs, and event venues. In October 2025, a female security guard at a Center City IHOP on Walnut Street fatally shot a male customer following a late-night dispute, as previously reported by FOX 29 Philadelphia. That same year, a banquet hall security guard in Germantown shot and killed a man armed with a knife outside Treasures Banquet Hall, an incident relayed by community safety advocates on Facebook and covered by 6abc. Nightlife violence in Philadelphia hasn't been limited to guard-involved shootings. In July 2025, a physical fight on an exterior balcony at 7 Elements bar and lounge in South Philadelphia escalated into a mass shooting that injured eight people, including two 43-year-old male security guards, according to WHYY. The Spring Garden corridor itself has seen prior violence: in February, federal marshals arrested a fugitive tied to a shooting on the 800 block of Spring Garden Street from November 2025 that left a bystander wounded during an outdoor altercation. Pennsylvania's Lethal Weapons Training Act, known as Act 235, requires any privately employed security guard who carries a firearm on duty to be certified by the Pennsylvania State Police after completing 40 hours of training, including legal authority instruction and physical and psychological exams, per the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. That certification does not substitute for a Pennsylvania License to Carry Firearms when it comes to off-duty carry, vehicle transit, or concealed carry, according to Pennsylvania State Police guidance tied to a 2017 Superior Court ruling. Philadelphia also imposes its own layer of training mandates. City Code Chapter 9-3700 requires bouncers and nightclub security personnel to complete 16 hours of approved third-party training covering nonviolent defense tactics, alcohol management, and age verification, and to register with the Department of Licenses and Inspections. The city passed a broader measure, Chapter 9-6800, in 2025 to mandate additional safety training for commercial security officers, but the Philadelphia Department of Labor announced in February that enforcement is postponed until city-approved training provider criteria are finalized. The Spring Garden shooting comes as overall gun violence in Philadelphia has fallen sharply this year. Philadelphia Police Department crime statistics through October 1 recorded 538 total shooting victims citywide, 113 of them fatal, marking roughly a 28% decrease in total shooting victims compared to the same period in 2025. The department also recorded 130 homicides through October 3, down nearly 22% from the 166 homicides reported over the equivalent stretch last year. Despite that citywide decline, the hunt for the guard who opened fire on Spring Garden Street underscores how quickly nightlife disputes can turn deadly even amid an improving crime picture. Philadelphia police have not released further details on the investigation or the condition of the man and woman who were involved in the initial confrontation. Nightlife violence in Philadelphia hasn't been limited to guard-involved shootings.

In October 2025, a female security guard at a Center City IHOP on Walnut Street fatally shot a male customer following a late-night dispute, as previously reported by FOX 29 Philadelphia.

extraction.body: A security guard is wanted by Philadelphia police after shooting a man during a confrontation outside a club on the 1000 block of Spring Garden Street early Sunday. The 39-year-old victim was taken to Jefferson Hospital and is listed in stable condition, while the guard fled the scene before officers could make an arrest. According to 6abc , the confrontation began around 12:30 a.m. when a man and a woman got into an argument with the security guard outside the club. Investigators say the guard pulled out a gun and shot the man before running from the scene. Police have not released the guard's identity, and the search for the suspect remains active. The shooting adds to a string of recent incidents in which armed security personnel have used lethal force during confrontations at Philadelphia bars, clubs, and event venues. In October 2025, a female security guard at a Center City IHOP on Walnut Street fatally shot a male customer following a late-night dispute, as previously reported by FOX 29 Philadelphia. That same year, a banquet hall security guard in Germantown shot and killed a man armed with a knife outside Treasures Banquet Hall, an incident relayed by community safety advocates on Facebook and covered by 6abc. Nightlife violence in Philadelphia hasn't been limited to guard-involved shootings. In July 2025, a physical fight on an exterior balcony at 7 Elements bar and lounge in South Philadelphia escalated into a mass shooting that injured eight people, including two 43-year-old male security guards, according to WHYY. The Spring Garden corridor itself has seen prior violence: in February, federal marshals arrested a fugitive tied to a shooting on the 800 block of Spring Garden Street from November 2025 that left a bystander wounded during an outdoor altercation. Pennsylvania's Lethal Weapons Training Act, known as Act 235, requires any privately employed security guard who carries a firearm on duty to be certified by the Pennsylvania State Police after completing 40 hours of training, including legal authority instruction and physical and psychological exams, per the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. That certification does not substitute for a Pennsylvania License to Carry Firearms when it comes to off-duty carry, vehicle transit, or concealed carry, according to Pennsylvania State Police guidance tied to a 2017 Superior Court ruling. Philadelphia also imposes its own layer of training mandates. City Code Chapter 9-3700 requires bouncers and nightclub security personnel to complete 16 hours of approved third-party training covering nonviolent defense tactics, alcohol management, and age verification, and to register with the Department of Licenses and Inspections. The city passed a broader measure, Chapter 9-6800, in 2025 to mandate additional safety training for commercial security officers, but the Philadelphia Department of Labor announced in February that enforcement is postponed until city-approved training provider criteria are finalized. The Spring Garden shooting comes as overall gun violence in Philadelphia has fallen sharply this year. Philadelphia Police Department crime statistics through October 1 recorded 538 total shooting victims citywide, 113 of them fatal, marking roughly a 28% decrease in total shooting victims compared to the same period in 2025. The department also recorded 130 homicides through October 3, down nearly 22% from the 166 homicides reported over the equivalent stretch last year. Despite that citywide decline, the hunt for the guard who opened fire on Spring Garden Street underscores how quickly nightlife disputes can turn deadly even amid an improving crime picture. Philadelphia police have not released further details on the investigation or the condition of the man and woman who were involved in the initial confrontation. sources.title: Apple says it’s tightening macOS ‘Full Disk Access’ controls due to new risks from AI agents
passages: Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS.
The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said.

sources.title: Google froze its open source bug bounty program due to a ‘significant rise’ in AI submissions
passages: Blaming a “significant rise” in AI submissions, Google has paused its open source bug bounty program until next year.
According to Tom’s Hardware , Google engineers and open source maintainers were overwhelmed by reports that were invalid or contained hallucinations.
Last year, TechCrunch reported that cybersecurity experts were warning of that AI slop posed a serious risk to bug bounty programs .
Looks like that’s the issue confronting Google’s Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program, where researchers were rewarded for finding vulnerabilities in the company’s open source software.

In posts on X and the program website , Google said the bug bounty program was paused as of October 1, with a promise to provide “an update” in the first quarter of 2027. extraction.body: Women hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruption Women hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruption T here’s a common fear among people who work in Silicon Valley: snag one of the fast-growing, high-paying jobs in artificial intelligence, or get trapped in the “permanent underclass”, a phrase describing the fate of those who won’t have upward mobility in the age of AI. The phrase usually describes a future in which AI automates human jobs. But for women in tech, it’s starting to look like the present. “A lot of people say: ‘Oh, AI is lowering barriers, it’s equalizing the playing field for women,’” said Urvashi Batra, co-founder and CEO of Prioriwise, an AI platform for IT service providers. “I actually think it’s the opposite.” Batra said people take her less seriously as the founder of an AI company than her male co-founder. When pitching investors, she and her co-founder have learned that they are more likely to get an investment if he does the pitching. Women made up only about a quarter of new hires in AI roles in the last year, compared to 50% of new hires in non-AI roles, according to a recent report from LinkedIn. In executive roles, that number drops to just 13%. At the same time, LinkedIn’s research shows that women are more likely to work in roles with high exposure to AI disruption, like customer service, meaning they are also at higher risk for job loss due to AI. AI jobs, whose postings have doubled since 2023, come with a salary premium, on average paying more than twice as much as roles that don’t involve working with AI, according to LinkedIn’s research. But women who do have jobs in AI are disproportionately concentrated in low-paying roles, like data annotators, said Sarah Steinberg, the head of global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn. Across all AI occupations, men have $45,000 higher median pay than women, partly due to the types of jobs they are likelier to have. “AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying and most consequential jobs in the global economy,” said Steinberg. “Women are just strikingly underrepresented.” The ongoing trend could produce the greatest gender pay gap in generations and leave women out of building a technology that shaped the economy, advocates for women in tech said. “What we’re witnessing is a sort of backsliding,” said Brenda Darden Wilkerson, president of AnitaB.org, a non-profit devoted to advancing women in tech jobs. Initiatives to promote women in the tech industry have been ongoing for years, with mixed results. Women now hold about one-third of tech jobs in the US. But research has found that women leave the tech industry at a much higher rate than their male counterparts, citing factors like non-inclusive cultures and barriers to advancement. Women working in AI may face even greater challenges. “AI moves extremely fast, and the pressure to keep up is immense,” said Jayeeta Putatunda, an AI engineering lead at investment firm Turing. “I have seen throughout my career so many amazing women I know kind of fall through the cracks.” Putatunda said it’s not uncommon to be the only female engineer on a team, and that when women are outnumbered, they have to speak up louder to make their ideas known. Mentorship in the AI field, especially by other women, can be hard to come by. And the breakneck pace of AI advancements means anyone working in the field should expect to put in long hours in order to keep up. “If you have very ambitious career goals in this field, there will be seasons when you work beyond normal hours,” she said, noting that a culture of working 12-hour days to keep up was not uncommon. “I don’t think there is always a neat shortcut around that than to put in the hours.” Those kinds of work expectations can make it impossible for everyone to stay in the field. “I went on maternity leave for four months , and by the time I came back, there were completely different frameworks and levels of models,” Putatunda said. Getting caught back up was overwhelming. She said it was only possible with the help of supportive co-workers and a husband who equitably split childcare. “That is one way women get pushed out of AI,” she said. “They don’t lack the interest or ability to keep up. They may lack the infrastructure that makes keeping up possible.” The AI industry is so new and fast-moving that it should in theory be more meritocratic. No one has a decade of experience working with a model developed one year ago, which should mean everyone has a level playing field. But instead the field has indexed more on personal networks and other loose signals, according to some women who work in AI. “Companies are hiring at a breakneck speed, but they’re finding people through the same networks, the same referrals, the same filters that they’ve always used,” Wilkerson said. “Generally, that’s not given women the same sort of exposure they should have.” When people have tried to address these tech industry problems in the past, the solutions have largely come down to giving women more mentorship and implementing diversity programs with goals around representation. But in recent years, companies have aggressively scaled back their diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs, largely in response to a political climate that discourages them. That has left fewer companies with institutional programs to hire and promote women. The political climate has made it more challenging to get AI companies to support initiatives focused on women, said Felicia Newhouse, founder of AI Powered Women, an organization that promotes women’s participation and leadership in AI. Newhouse, a product marketer who has worked in technology companies for two decades, points to the Department of Justice targeting corporations with DEI programs, claiming the initiatives violate anti-discrimination laws. Companies like Accenture, Deloitte, IBM and PayPal have all agreed to pay multimillion-dollar settlements under this enforcement. “It is getting harder to go into companies being called AI Powered Women,” Newhouse said. “And our advocates inside those companies are also struggling with having women-focused initiatives.” Still, she said the risk that women are left behind in the AI workforce was something that kept her up at night. “We’re talking about who captures a major new source of economic mobility,” she said. “The deepest risk is that a participation gap becomes a power gap.”
